title: Part 3, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Razumihin woke the next morning at eight o'clock, troubled and serious. He found himself faced with many new and unexpected complications. He had never imagined he would wake up feeling like this. He remembered every detail of the previous day and knew that something entirely novel had happened to him, that he had experienced an impression unlike anything he had ever known. At the same time he clearly recognized that the dream firing his imagination was hopelessly unattainable -- so unattainable that he was actually ashamed of it and quickly turned his thoughts to the more practical worries and problems left behind by that "thrice-accursed yesterday."

The most awful memory from the day before was how "base and vile" he had shown himself -- not only because he was drunk, but because he had exploited the young woman's situation to abuse her _fiancé_ out of jealous stupidity, knowing nothing about their mutual relations and obligations and next to nothing about the man himself. What right did he have to criticize him so hastily and rudely? Who had asked for his opinion? Was it even conceivable that a creature like Avdotya Romanovna would marry an unworthy man for money? So there must be something worthwhile in him. And the lodgings? How could he have known what the rooms were like? After all, the man was furnishing an apartment... God, how contemptible it all was! What kind of excuse was being drunk? That stupid defense was even more degrading! In wine is truth, and the truth had all come out -- "the ugliness of his coarse, jealous heart"! And would such a dream ever be permissible for him, Razumihin? What was he compared to such a woman -- he, the drunken loudmouth from last night? Was such an absurd, cynical comparison even thinkable? Razumihin blushed desperately, and suddenly the memory forced itself upon him of how he had said on the stairs that the landlady would be jealous of Avdotya Romanovna... That was simply unbearable. He slammed his fist down on the kitchen stove, hurt his hand, and sent a brick flying.

"Of course," he muttered to himself a minute later, with a feeling of self-disgust, "of course none of these disgraces can ever be wiped out or made right... so there's no point even thinking about it. I must go to them in silence and do my duty... in silence too... and not ask forgiveness, and say nothing... because all is lost now!"

And yet, as he dressed, he examined his clothes more carefully than usual. He had no other suit -- and if he had, he might have deliberately not worn it. "I would have made a point of not putting it on." Still, he could not remain a cynic and a slob. He had no right to offend other people's feelings, especially when they needed his help and had asked to see him. He brushed his clothes carefully. His linen was always decent; in that respect he was especially clean.

That morning he washed meticulously -- he got soap from Nastasya -- scrubbing his hair, his neck, and especially his hands. When it came to whether or not to shave his stubbled chin (Praskovya Pavlovna had excellent razors left by her late husband), the question was answered furiously in the negative. "Let it stay as it is! What if they think I shaved on purpose to... They'd certainly think so! Not a chance!"

"And... the worst of it was that he was so coarse, so dirty, with tavern manners; and... and even assuming he knew he had some of the basics of a gentleman... what was there to be proud of in that? Everyone ought to be a gentleman, and more than that... And all the same (he remembered) he too had done some things... not exactly dishonest, but still.... And what thoughts he sometimes had; hmm... and to set all that beside Avdotya Romanovna! Confound it! So be it! Well, he'd make a point of being dirty, greasy, tavern-mannered -- and he wouldn't care! He'd be even worse!"
He was in the middle of these monologues when Zossimov, who had spent the night in Praskovya Pavlovna's parlor, came in.

He was on his way home and wanted to check on the patient first. Razumihin told him Raskolnikov was sleeping like a log. Zossimov gave orders not to wake him and promised to look in again around eleven.
"If he's still home," he added. "Damn it all! How can you treat patients if you can't control them? Do you know whether _he_ will go to _them_, or _they_ are coming here?"

"They're coming, I think," Razumihin said, understanding the implied question, "and they'll discuss family matters, no doubt. I'll clear out. You, as the doctor, have more right to be here than I do."
"But I'm not a confessor. I'll come, take a look, and leave. I have plenty to do besides looking after them."

"One thing worries me," Razumihin said, frowning. "On the way home last night I talked a lot of drunken nonsense to him... all sorts of things... including that you were afraid he might... go insane."
"You told the ladies too."
"I know -- it was stupid! You can hit me if you want! Did you really think so?"

"Nonsense, I tell you. How could I have seriously thought that? _You_ described him as a monomaniac when you brought me to see him... and then we poured fuel on the fire yesterday -- you did, that is -- with the story about the painter. A fine subject for conversation, when that may have been the very thing he was fixated on! If I'd known what happened at the police station, that some wretch... had insulted him with this suspicion! Hmm... I would never have allowed that conversation yesterday. These monomaniacs make mountains out of molehills... they see their fantasies as solid reality.... As far as I recall, Zametov's story cleared up half the puzzle for me. I know of a case where a forty-year-old hypochondriac cut the throat of an eight-year-old boy because he couldn't stand the boy's daily teasing at dinner! And in this case -- his rags, the rude policeman, the fever, this suspicion! All working on a man half-deranged by hypochondria, with his morbid, exceptional pride! That may well have been what triggered the illness. Well, to hell with it all!... And by the way, that Zametov is actually a nice enough lad, but hmm... he shouldn't have blabbed all that last night. He's an awful chatterbox!"
"But who did he tell? You and me?"
"And Porfiry."
"So what?"
"By the way, do you have any influence on them -- his mother and sister? Tell them to be more careful with him today...."
"They'll be fine!" Razumihin replied reluctantly.
"And why is he so set against this Luzhin? A man with money, and she doesn't seem to dislike him... and they haven't got a kopeck themselves, I suppose? Eh?"
"What business is it of yours?" Razumihin snapped with annoyance. "How should I know whether they've got a kopeck? Ask them yourself and maybe you'll find out...."

"God, what an ass you can be sometimes! Last night's wine hasn't worn off yet.... Goodbye. Thank your Praskovya Pavlovna for me for the night's lodging. She locked herself in and didn't answer my _bonjour_ through the door. She was up at seven -- the samovar was brought to her from the kitchen. I was not granted a personal audience...."

At nine o'clock sharp, Razumihin arrived at the lodgings in Bakaleyev's house. Both ladies were waiting for him with nervous impatience. They had been up since seven or earlier. He walked in looking black as night, bowed awkwardly, and immediately cursed himself for it. He had not reckoned on this: Pulcheria Alexandrovna practically threw herself at him, seized both his hands, and nearly kissed them. He glanced timidly at Avdotya Romanovna, but her proud face wore an expression of such gratitude and warmth, such complete and unexpected respect (instead of the sneering looks and barely concealed contempt he had expected), that it threw him into even greater confusion than insults would have. Fortunately there was a topic ready at hand, and he seized on it eagerly.

Learning that everything was going well and Rodya had not yet woken, Pulcheria Alexandrovna declared she was glad, because "there was something very, very important she needed to discuss beforehand." Then came the question of breakfast and an invitation to share it with them. They had waited to eat with him. Avdotya Romanovna rang the bell. A ragged, dirty waiter appeared, and they ordered tea, which was eventually served in such filthy, chaotic fashion that the ladies were embarrassed. Razumihin launched a vigorous attack on the lodgings but, remembering Luzhin, stopped himself in embarrassment. He was greatly relieved when Pulcheria Alexandrovna's questions came pouring down on him in a steady stream.

He talked for three-quarters of an hour, constantly interrupted by their questions, and managed to describe all the most important facts he knew of Raskolnikov's life over the past year, ending with a detailed account of his illness. He left out a good deal that was better left unmentioned, including the scene at the police station with all its consequences. They listened eagerly, and when he thought he had finished and satisfied his audience, he discovered they felt he had barely started.
"Tell me, tell me! What do you think...? Excuse me, I still don't know your name!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna said hurriedly.
"Dmitri Prokofitch."

"I'd very, very much like to know, Dmitri Prokofitch... how he looks at things in general now, that is, how can I put it, what are his likes and dislikes? Is he always this irritable? Tell me, if you can, what his hopes and, so to speak, his dreams are? What influences him now? In a word, I'd like..."
"Mama, how can he answer all of that at once?" Dounia observed.
"Good heavens -- I never expected to find him in the least like this, Dmitri Prokofitch!"

"Naturally," Razumihin replied. "I have no mother, but my uncle comes every year and almost every time he can barely recognize me, even just my appearance -- and he's a sharp man. Your three years' separation makes a big difference. What can I tell you? I've known Rodion for a year and a half. He's moody, gloomy, proud, and arrogant -- and lately, perhaps for a long time now, suspicious and prone to dark fancies. He has a noble nature and a kind heart. He doesn't like showing his feelings and would rather act cruelly than open up. Sometimes, though, he isn't morbid at all -- just cold and inhumanly callous, as though two completely different characters were taking turns inside him. Sometimes he's terrifyingly uncommunicative! He says he's so busy that everything is in his way, and yet he lies on his bed doing nothing. He doesn't mock things -- not because he lacks the wit, but as though he can't waste time on trifles. He never listens to what people say. He's never interested in what interests others at any given moment. He thinks very highly of himself, and perhaps he has a right to. Well, what more? I think your arrival will have an extremely positive effect on him."
"God grant it!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, distressed by Razumihin's portrait of her Rodya.

And at last Razumihin ventured to look more openly at Avdotya Romanovna. He had been glancing at her throughout his account, but only for a moment before looking away each time. Avdotya Romanovna had been sitting at the table, listening closely, then had gotten up and resumed her pacing -- arms folded, lips pressed together, occasionally putting in a question without breaking stride. She too had a habit of not fully attending to what was being said. She wore a dress of thin, dark fabric and a white transparent scarf around her neck. Razumihin quickly noticed signs of extreme poverty in their belongings. Had Avdotya Romanovna been dressed like a queen, he would probably not have been afraid of her at all. But perhaps precisely because she was poorly dressed, and because he noticed the shabbiness all around them, his heart filled with dread and he began fearing every word, every gesture -- which was very hard on a man who already felt unsure of himself.

"You've told us a great deal that is interesting about my brother's character... and told it impartially. I'm glad. I had thought you were too uncritically devoted to him," Avdotya Romanovna observed with a smile. "I think you're right that he needs a woman's care," she added thoughtfully.
"I didn't say that exactly, but I daresay you're right, only..."
"What?"
"He loves no one and perhaps never will," Razumihin declared flatly.
"You mean he's incapable of love?"

"You know, Avdotya Romanovna, you're remarkably like your brother -- in everything!" he blurted out, surprising even himself. But then, remembering what he had just said about her brother, he turned red as a lobster and was overcome with confusion. Avdotya Romanovna could not help laughing at the sight of him.

"You may both be wrong about Rodya," Pulcheria Alexandrovna put in, slightly stung. "I'm not talking about the present situation, Dounia. What Pyotr Petrovitch writes in this letter and what you and I assumed may be mistaken. But you can't imagine, Dmitri Prokofitch, how moody and -- what's the word -- unpredictable he is. I could never count on what he would do, even when he was only fifteen. And I'm sure he could do something now that nobody else would ever think of doing... For instance, do you know how he stunned me, gave me a shock that nearly killed me, a year and a half ago, when he decided to marry that girl -- what was her name -- his landlady's daughter?"
"Did you hear about that?" Avdotya Romanovna asked.

"Do you suppose --" Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on warmly. "Do you suppose that my tears, my pleading, my illness, my possible death from grief, or our poverty would have stopped him? Not at all! He would have calmly stepped over every obstacle. And yet it isn't that he doesn't love us!"
"He never said a word to me about it," Razumihin answered cautiously, "but I did hear something from Praskovya Pavlovna herself -- and she's not one to gossip. What I heard was certainly rather odd."
"And what did you hear?" both ladies asked at once.

"Nothing very extraordinary. I only learned that the marriage -- which fell through only because the girl died -- was not at all to Praskovya Pavlovna's liking. They say the girl was not particularly attractive -- in fact, I'm told, positively ugly... and rather sickly... and strange. But she seems to have had some good qualities. She must have had some good qualities, or it's quite inexplicable.... She had no money either, and he wouldn't have been influenced by money.... But it's always hard to judge in such matters."
"I'm sure she was a good person," Avdotya Romanovna said briefly.

"God forgive me, but I simply rejoiced at her death. Though I don't know which of them would have caused more misery to the other -- he to her, or she to him," Pulcheria Alexandrovna concluded. Then, tentatively, she began questioning him about the previous day's scene with Luzhin, hesitating and continually glancing at Dounia -- obviously to the latter's annoyance. This episode more than anything else was causing her worry, even alarm. Razumihin went through it all again in detail, but this time he added his own assessment: he openly blamed Raskolnikov for deliberately insulting Pyotr Petrovitch, and did not try to excuse him on grounds of illness.
"He had planned it before his illness," he added.

"I think so too," Pulcheria Alexandrovna agreed with a dejected air. But she was very surprised to hear Razumihin speak so carefully and even respectfully about Pyotr Petrovitch. Avdotya Romanovna was struck by it too.
"So this is your opinion of Pyotr Petrovitch?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna could not resist asking.

"I can't have any other opinion of your daughter's future husband," Razumihin said firmly and with warmth. "And I don't say it merely out of politeness, but because... simply because Avdotya Romanovna has of her own free will chosen to accept this man. If I spoke rudely about him last night, it was because I was disgustingly drunk and... out of my mind. Yes -- mad, out of my mind, and this morning I'm ashamed of it."
He turned crimson and fell silent. Avdotya Romanovna blushed too but did not break the silence. She had not uttered a word from the moment they began discussing Luzhin.
Without her support, Pulcheria Alexandrovna was clearly at a loss. At last, faltering and constantly glancing at her daughter, she confessed that one thing was troubling her terribly.
"You see, Dmitri Prokofitch," she began. "I'll be perfectly frank with Dmitri Prokofitch -- shall I, Dounia?"
"Of course, Mama," Avdotya Romanovna said emphatically.

"Here's the thing," she began hastily, as though the permission to discuss her worry lifted a weight from her shoulders. "Very early this morning we received a note from Pyotr Petrovitch, in reply to our letter announcing our arrival. He had promised to meet us at the station, you know, but instead he sent a servant to bring us the address of these lodgings and show us the way. Along with that, he sent word that he would come here himself this morning. But this morning, this note arrived from him. You'd better read it yourself. There's one point that greatly concerns me... you'll see which one right away... and please tell me your honest opinion, Dmitri Prokofitch! You know Rodya's character better than anyone, and no one can advise us better. I should tell you, Dounia made her decision at once, but I still don't know what to do, and I... I've been waiting for your opinion."
Razumihin unfolded the note, which was dated the previous evening, and read as follows:

"Dear Madam, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, I have the honor to inform you that owing to unforeseen obstacles, I was unable to meet you at the railway station. I sent a very capable person in my place. I shall likewise be unable to have the honor of an interview with you tomorrow morning, as I have business in the Senate that cannot be delayed, and also because I do not wish to intrude upon your family circle while you are greeting your son and Avdotya Romanovna her brother. I shall have the honor of visiting and paying my respects at your lodgings no later than tomorrow evening at eight o'clock precisely. Herewith I venture to present my earnest and, I may add, imperative request that Rodion Romanovitch not be present at our meeting, as he offered me a gross and unprecedented insult during my visit to him yesterday, and furthermore, as I wish to obtain from you personally an indispensable and detailed explanation of a certain matter, regarding which I desire to hear your own interpretation. I have the honor to inform you in advance that if, in spite of my request, I meet Rodion Romanovitch, I shall be compelled to withdraw immediately, and then you will have only yourself to blame. I write on the assumption that Rodion Romanovitch, who seemed so ill during my visit, suddenly recovered two hours later, and therefore, being well enough to leave the house, may visit you as well. I was confirmed in this belief by the evidence of my own eyes in the lodging of a drunkard who had been run over and subsequently died, to whose daughter, a young woman of notorious character, he gave twenty-five rubles on the pretext of funeral expenses -- which greatly surprised me, knowing the pains it cost you to raise that sum. With particular respect to your estimable daughter, Avdotya Romanovna, I beg you to accept the respectful homage of
"Your humble servant,
"P. LUZHIN."

"What should I do now, Dmitri Prokofitch?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, nearly in tears. "How can I ask Rodya not to come? Yesterday he insisted so forcefully that we refuse Pyotr Petrovitch, and now we're ordered not to receive Rodya! If he finds out, he'll come on purpose, and then... what will happen?"
"Do whatever Avdotya Romanovna decides," Razumihin answered at once, calmly.

"Oh, dear! She says... goodness knows what she says, and she won't explain herself! She says it would be best -- not that it would be best, but that it's absolutely necessary -- for Rodya to make a point of being here at eight o'clock, and that they must meet.... I didn't even want to show him the letter. I thought we could somehow prevent him from coming, with your help... because he's so irritable.... Besides, I don't understand the part about the drunkard who died and the daughter, and how he could have given her all the money... which..."
"Which cost you such sacrifice, Mama," Avdotya Romanovna put in.

"He wasn't himself yesterday," Razumihin said thoughtfully. "If you only knew what he got up to in a restaurant yesterday -- though there was some sense in it too.... Hmm! He did say something as we walked home about a dead man and a girl, but I couldn't make sense of it.... Though last night I myself..."

"The best thing, Mama, will be for us to go see him ourselves, and I'm sure we'll immediately see what needs to be done. Besides, it's getting late -- good heavens, it's past ten!" she cried, glancing at a beautiful gold enameled watch that hung around her neck on a thin Venetian chain and was completely out of place with the rest of her outfit. "A gift from her _fiancé_," Razumihin thought.
"We must go, Dounia, we must go," her mother said in a flutter. "He'll think we're still angry about yesterday, since we're so late. Oh, dear!"

While saying this she was hastily putting on her hat and cloak. Dounia put on hers too. Her gloves, Razumihin noticed, were not merely shabby but had holes in them -- yet this obvious poverty gave both women an air of special dignity, which is always found in people who know how to wear poor clothes well. Razumihin gazed reverently at Dounia and felt proud to be escorting her. "Marie Antoinette, the queen who darned stockings in prison," he thought, "must have looked every inch a queen in that moment, even more than at state banquets."
"My God!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed. "Little did I think I'd ever be afraid to see my own son -- my darling, darling Rodya! I'm afraid, Dmitri Prokofitch," she added, glancing at him timidly.
"Don't be afraid, Mama," Dounia said, kissing her. "Better to have faith in him."
"Oh, I do have faith in him, but I haven't slept all night!" the poor woman cried.
They stepped out into the street.

"You know, Dounia, when I dozed off a little this morning, I dreamed of Marfa Petrovna... she was all in white... she came up to me, took my hand, and shook her head at me -- so sternly, as though she were blaming me.... Is that a good sign? Oh, dear! You don't know, Dmitri Prokofitch -- Marfa Petrovna's dead!"
"No, I didn't know. Who is Marfa Petrovna?"
"She died suddenly -- just imagine..."
"Later, Mama," Dounia put in. "He doesn't know who Marfa Petrovna is."

"Oh, you don't know? And I was thinking you knew all about us. Forgive me, Dmitri Prokofitch -- I've lost track of what I'm thinking these last few days. I truly regard you as our guardian angel, and so I assumed you knew everything. I think of you as family.... Don't be angry with me for saying that. Oh dear, what's the matter with your right hand? Did you hurt it?"
"Yes, I bruised it," muttered Razumihin, overjoyed.

"I sometimes speak too much from the heart -- Dounia scolds me for it.... But, dear me, what a closet he lives in! I wonder if he's awake yet? Does this woman, his landlady, really consider that a room? Listen, you say he doesn't like showing his feelings -- so perhaps I'll annoy him with my... weakness? Please advise me, Dmitri Prokofitch. How should I behave with him? I feel completely at a loss, you know."
"Don't question him too much about anything if you see him frown. Don't ask too much about his health -- he doesn't like that."
"Oh, Dmitri Prokofitch, how hard it is to be a mother! But here are the stairs.... What a dreadful staircase!"
"Mama, you're quite pale. Don't distress yourself, darling," Dounia said, caressing her. Then, with flashing eyes, she added: "He ought to be happy to see you, and you're tormenting yourself."
"Wait -- let me peek in and see if he's awake."

The ladies slowly followed Razumihin, who went ahead. When they reached the landlady's door on the fourth floor, they noticed it was cracked open and two keen black eyes were watching them from the darkness. When their eyes met, the door was suddenly slammed shut with such force that Pulcheria Alexandrovna nearly cried out.
